description: The Wolfram Language implements several hundred mathematical functions with full symbolic knowledge (derivatives, integrals, series, identities and branch cut structure) and arbitrary-precision numeric evaluation over the whole complex plane. Nearly all of them are Listable, so they thread automatically over arrays. This category covers the elementary functions and the most widely used special functions.

tools.name: Exp
tools.description: The exponential function E^z, evaluated exactly for special arguments and numerically to any precision elsewhere. It is Listable and defined for complex arguments, where Exp[I x] gives Cos[x] + I Sin[x]. For matrices use MatrixExp, which is a different operation.
tools.example:
Exp[0]
Exp[1] // N
Exp[I Pi]
N[Exp[1], 50]
Exp[{0, 1, 2}]
tools.notes: Writing E^z and Exp[z] gives the same expression internally. Exp[x] applied to a matrix acts elementwise; MatrixExp is the matrix exponential.

tools.name: Log
tools.description: The natural logarithm, with Log[b, z] giving the logarithm to base b. For complex arguments it returns the principal value with a branch cut along the negative real axis. Log of a negative real gives a complex result rather than an error.
tools.notes: PowerExpand rewrites Log[a b] as Log[a] + Log[b] but ignores branch cuts; use Simplify with positivity assumptions when correctness matters.

tools.name: Log10
tools.description: The base-10 logarithm, with Log2 the base-2 counterpart. Both are shorthands for Log[b, z] that evaluate exactly on exact powers of the base. They are Listable and commonly used for decibel, pH and order-of-magnitude computations.

tools.name: Power
tools.description: Raises a number or expression to a power, written infix as x^y. It handles integer, rational, real, complex and symbolic exponents, giving the principal value for fractional powers of negative numbers. Power is Listable, so it operates elementwise on arrays rather than as a matrix power.
tools.notes: (-8)^(1/3) gives the principal complex root; Surd[-8, 3] gives the real cube root -2. Use MatrixPower for matrix exponentiation.

tools.name: Sqrt
tools.description: The square root, equivalent to z^(1/2) and returning the principal branch with a cut along the negative real axis. It stays exact for perfect squares and simplifies surds partially, so Sqrt[8] gives 2 Sqrt[2]. Sqrt of a negative real gives an imaginary result.
tools.example:
Sqrt[16]
Sqrt[8]
Sqrt[-4]
N[Sqrt[2], 40]
Simplify[Sqrt[x^2], x > 0]
tools.notes: Sqrt[x^2] does not simplify to x without an assumption that x is non-negative, because the identity fails for negative and complex x.

tools.name: Sin
tools.description: The sine function with argument in radians, evaluated exactly at rational multiples of Pi and numerically to any precision elsewhere. It is Listable, defined for complex arguments, and carries full symbolic knowledge of its derivatives, integrals and series. Use Degree to work in degrees, as in Sin[30 Degree].
tools.example:
Sin[Pi/2]
Sin[Pi/6]
Sin[30 Degree]
N[Sin[1], 30]
Sin[{0, Pi/2, Pi}]
tools.notes: Arguments are always in radians unless multiplied by Degree. Sin[x]^2 + Cos[x]^2 simplifies to 1 under Simplify.

tools.name: Cos
tools.description: The cosine function with argument in radians, exact at rational multiples of Pi and numerically evaluable to arbitrary precision. Like all trigonometric functions it is Listable and defined throughout the complex plane. Cos[I x] equals Cosh[x], linking it to the hyperbolic functions.
tools.example:
Cos[0]
Cos[Pi/3]
Cos[60 Degree]
Cos[I]
Plot[Cos[x], {x, 0, 2 Pi}]

tools.name: Tan
tools.description: The tangent function, Sin[z]/Cos[z], with poles at odd multiples of Pi/2 where it evaluates to ComplexInfinity. Cot, Sec and Csc complete the set of six trigonometric functions. All are exact at rational multiples of Pi and Listable.
tools.example:
Tan[Pi/4]
Tan[Pi/2]
Cot[Pi/4]
Sec[0]
N[Tan[1], 20]

tools.name: ArcSin
tools.description: The inverse sine, returning a principal value in the range -Pi/2 to Pi/2 for real arguments in [-1, 1] and complex values outside that range. It has branch cuts on the real axis beyond ±1. Exact results are returned for the standard special values.
tools.example:
ArcSin[1]
ArcSin[1/2]
ArcSin[0.5] / Degree
ArcSin[2]
D[ArcSin[x], x]

tools.name: ArcCos
tools.description: The inverse cosine, giving principal values in the range 0 to Pi for real arguments in [-1, 1]. Outside that interval the result is complex, with branch cuts beyond ±1 on the real axis. It is the standard way to recover an angle from a normalized dot product.
tools.example:
ArcCos[0]
ArcCos[-1]
ArcCos[Sqrt[3]/2]
ArcCos[u . v/(Norm[u] Norm[v])]
ArcCos[0.3] / Degree

tools.name: ArcTan
tools.description: The inverse tangent, returning values in -Pi/2 to Pi/2 for the one-argument form. The two-argument form ArcTan[x, y] gives the angle of the point (x, y) measured from the positive x axis over the full range -Pi to Pi, correctly handling all four quadrants. Always prefer the two-argument form for converting Cartesian coordinates to an angle.
tools.example:
ArcTan[1]
ArcTan[-1, -1]
ArcTan[1, 1]
ArcTan[0, 1]
ArcTan[y, x] // N
tools.notes: ArcTan[x, y] is the equivalent of atan2(y, x) in other languages, but note the reversed argument order: x comes first.

tools.name: Sinh
tools.description: The hyperbolic sine, (Exp[z] - Exp[-z])/2, defined for all complex arguments and Listable. It is related to the circular sine by Sinh[z] == -I Sin[I z]. Together with Cosh it describes catenaries, relativistic rapidity and the solutions of many linear ODEs.
tools.example:
Sinh[0]
Sinh[1.] 
Sinh[I Pi/2]
TrigToExp[Sinh[x]]
D[Sinh[x], x]

tools.name: Cosh
tools.description: The hyperbolic cosine, (Exp[z] + Exp[-z])/2, with minimum value 1 at the origin for real arguments. It is the shape of a hanging chain and appears throughout the solutions of second-order linear equations. Cosh[z]^2 - Sinh[z]^2 == 1 is the hyperbolic Pythagorean identity.
tools.example:
Cosh[0]
Cosh[1.]
Simplify[Cosh[x]^2 - Sinh[x]^2]
Plot[Cosh[x], {x, -3, 3}]

tools.name: Tanh
tools.description: The hyperbolic tangent, Sinh[z]/Cosh[z], a smooth sigmoid mapping the real line onto (-1, 1). Coth, Sech and Csch complete the hyperbolic family. Tanh is heavily used as a saturating nonlinearity and as a smooth step function.
tools.example:
Tanh[0]
Tanh[10.]
Limit[Tanh[x], x -> Infinity]
Sech[0]
Plot[Tanh[x], {x, -5, 5}]

tools.name: ArcTanh
tools.description: The inverse hyperbolic tangent, with ArcSinh, ArcCosh, ArcCoth, ArcSech and ArcCsch completing the inverse hyperbolic family. ArcTanh is real on (-1, 1) and has logarithmic branch points at ±1. These functions appear as the results of many rational integrals.
tools.example:
ArcTanh[0]
ArcTanh[1/2]
ArcSinh[1]
TrigToExp[ArcTanh[x]]
Integrate[1/(1 - x^2), x]

tools.name: Gamma
tools.description: The Euler gamma function, the analytic continuation of the factorial with Gamma[n + 1] == n!. The two- and three-argument forms give the upper and generalized incomplete gamma functions. It has simple poles at the non-positive integers and is fundamental to probability distributions and special function identities.
tools.usage:
Gamma[z]
Gamma[a, z]
Gamma[a, z0, z1]
tools.example:
Gamma[5]
Gamma[1/2]
Gamma[5/2]
Gamma[2, 3.]
N[Gamma[10.5], 20]
tools.notes: For large arguments use LogGamma to avoid overflow, and Beta for the ratio combinations that occur in distributions.

tools.name: LogGamma
tools.description: The logarithm of the gamma function, computed directly so that it remains finite for large arguments where Gamma itself overflows. On the positive real axis it is the ordinary real logarithm of Gamma; in the complex plane it is the continuous branch, which differs from Log[Gamma[z]]. It is the standard building block for log-likelihoods involving factorials.
tools.example:
LogGamma[10]
LogGamma[1000.]
Exp[LogGamma[5]]
LogGamma[1/2]
N[LogGamma[10^6]]
tools.notes: Use LogGamma rather than Log[Gamma[x]] in numerical code: Gamma[1000.] overflows machine range while LogGamma[1000.] does not.

tools.name: PolyGamma
tools.description: The digamma function PolyGamma[z] is the logarithmic derivative of Gamma, and PolyGamma[n, z] gives the n-th derivative of the digamma. These appear as the derivatives of log-likelihoods, in harmonic number identities and in the expansions of many series. PolyGamma[0, n+1] equals HarmonicNumber[n] - EulerGamma.
tools.example:
PolyGamma[1]
PolyGamma[1, 1]
PolyGamma[0, 5] // FunctionExpand
D[LogGamma[x], x]
N[PolyGamma[2, 3], 20]

tools.name: Beta
tools.description: The Euler beta function Beta[a, b] == Gamma[a] Gamma[b]/Gamma[a + b]. The three-argument Beta[z, a, b] is the incomplete beta function, and BetaRegularized is its normalized form, which is the CDF of the beta distribution. These are the core functions behind the beta, binomial and Student t distributions.
tools.usage:
Beta[a, b]
Beta[z, a, b]
BetaRegularized[z, a, b]
tools.example:
Beta[2, 3]
Beta[1/2, 1/2]
Beta[0.5, 2, 3]
BetaRegularized[0.5, 2, 3]
CDF[BetaDistribution[2, 3], 0.5]

tools.name: Erf
tools.description: The error function, 2/Sqrt[Pi] times the integral of Exp[-t^2] from 0 to z. It is the basic special function of Gaussian probability, with Erf[Infinity] == 1. The two-argument form Erf[z0, z1] gives the integral between two limits.
tools.example:
Erf[0]
Erf[1.]
Erf[Infinity]
Integrate[Exp[-t^2], {t, 0, x}]
Erf[0, 1] // N
tools.notes: The normal CDF is (1 + Erf[(x - mu)/(sigma Sqrt[2])])/2; for the far tail use Erfc to avoid cancellation.

tools.name: Erfc
tools.description: The complementary error function 1 - Erf[z], computed directly so it stays accurate in the far tail where 1 - Erf[z] would lose all significant digits. InverseErf and InverseErfc give the corresponding inverse functions, used to convert probabilities into quantiles. Erfi is the imaginary error function.
tools.example:
Erfc[0]
Erfc[5.]
1 - Erf[5.]
InverseErfc[0.05]
Erfi[1.]
tools.notes: Erfc[5.] is about 1.5*10^-12 while 1 - Erf[5.] loses most of its digits to cancellation; always use Erfc for tail probabilities.

tools.name: Zeta
tools.description: The Riemann zeta function, with the two-argument form Zeta[s, a] giving the Hurwitz zeta. It evaluates exactly at even positive integers and at negative integers, and to arbitrary precision elsewhere including on the critical line. ZetaZero gives the nontrivial zeros directly.
tools.example:
Zeta[2]
Zeta[4]
Zeta[-1]
N[Zeta[1/2 + 14.1347 I]]
N[ZetaZero[1], 20]

tools.name: PolyLog
tools.description: The polylogarithm function PolyLog[n, z], the sum of z^k/k^n, which reduces to -Log[1-z] for n == 1 and to Zeta[n] at z == 1. The Nielsen generalized form PolyLog[n, p, z] is also available. Polylogarithms arise in the evaluation of many integrals and in statistical mechanics.
tools.example:
PolyLog[2, 1]
PolyLog[1, z]
PolyLog[2, 0.5]
Integrate[Log[1 - t]/t, {t, 0, x}]
Series[PolyLog[2, z], {z, 0, 4}]

tools.name: HarmonicNumber
tools.description: The n-th harmonic number, the sum of 1/k for k from 1 to n, extended to non-integer and complex arguments through the digamma function. HarmonicNumber[n, r] gives the generalized harmonic number with exponent r. It appears constantly in the analysis of algorithms and in discrete sums.
tools.example:
HarmonicNumber[5]
HarmonicNumber[10.]
HarmonicNumber[4, 2]
Asymptotic[HarmonicNumber[n], n -> Infinity]
Sum[1/k, {k, 1, n}]

tools.name: ProductLog
tools.description: The Lambert W function, the inverse of z Exp[z], with ProductLog[k, z] selecting branch k. It is the closed-form solution of equations of the form x Exp[x] == a, which appear in delay equations, tree enumeration and iterated exponentials. On the real axis the principal branch is real for z >= -1/E.
tools.example:
ProductLog[0]
ProductLog[E]
Solve[x Exp[x] == 2, x]
N[ProductLog[-1, -0.1]]
ProductLog[1.]
tools.notes: Solve returns ProductLog for transcendental equations of this shape; N then gives a numerical value on the requested branch.

tools.name: BesselJ
tools.description: The Bessel function of the first kind J_n(z), the solution of Bessel's equation that is regular at the origin. It describes vibrations of circular membranes, cylindrical wave propagation and diffraction patterns. Orders may be integer, half-integer, real or complex, and half-integer orders reduce to elementary functions.
tools.example:
BesselJ[0, 0]
BesselJ[0, 2.4048]
FunctionExpand[BesselJ[1/2, x]]
BesselJZero[0, 1] // N
Plot[BesselJ[0, x], {x, 0, 20}]
tools.notes: BesselJZero[n, k] gives the k-th positive zero, which is what you need for eigenvalues of a circular drum.

tools.name: BesselY
tools.description: The Bessel function of the second kind Y_n(z), the solution of Bessel's equation that is singular at the origin. Together with BesselJ it gives the general solution for cylindrical problems on annular domains where the origin is excluded. It diverges logarithmically as z approaches 0.
tools.example:
BesselY[0, 1.]
BesselY[1, 2.]
Limit[BesselY[0, x], x -> 0]
BesselYZero[0, 1] // N

tools.name: BesselI
tools.description: The modified Bessel function of the first kind I_n(z), which grows exponentially for large real arguments. It solves the modified Bessel equation and appears in problems with exponential rather than oscillatory radial behaviour, such as steady heat conduction in cylinders and the von Mises distribution.
tools.example:
BesselI[0, 0]
BesselI[0, 1.]
BesselI[1, 2.]
Series[BesselI[0, x], {x, 0, 4}]

tools.name: BesselK
tools.description: The modified Bessel function of the second kind K_n(z), which decays exponentially for large positive arguments and diverges at the origin. It is the decaying solution used for exterior problems and for screened potentials. K_n also appears as the kernel of several heavy-tailed probability distributions.
tools.example:
BesselK[0, 1.]
BesselK[1, 2.]
Limit[BesselK[0, x], x -> Infinity]
Asymptotic[BesselK[0, x], x -> Infinity]

tools.name: AiryAi
tools.description: The Airy function Ai(z), the solution of y'' == z y that decays for large positive z. AiryBi is the complementary growing solution, and AiryAiPrime and AiryBiPrime give the derivatives. Airy functions describe turning points in WKB analysis, quantum tunnelling and optical caustics.
tools.example:
AiryAi[0]
AiryAi[1.]
AiryBi[0]
N[AiryAiZero[1], 15]
DSolve[y''[x] == x y[x], y[x], x]

tools.name: LegendreP
tools.description: The Legendre polynomials P_n(x) and, in the three-argument form, the associated Legendre functions P_n^m(x). They are orthogonal on [-1, 1] and are the angular part of solutions to Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates. LegendreQ gives the second-kind solutions.
tools.usage:
LegendreP[n, x]
LegendreP[n, m, x]
LegendreQ[n, x]
tools.example:
LegendreP[3, x]
Table[LegendreP[n, x], {n, 0, 4}]
LegendreP[2, 1, x]
Integrate[LegendreP[2, x] LegendreP[3, x], {x, -1, 1}]
SphericalHarmonicY[2, 1, th, ph]
tools.notes: Gauss-Legendre quadrature nodes are the roots of LegendreP[n, x], obtainable with NSolve or Root.

tools.name: HermiteH
tools.description: The physicists' Hermite polynomials H_n(x), orthogonal on the whole real line with weight Exp[-x^2]. They give the eigenfunctions of the quantum harmonic oscillator when multiplied by a Gaussian. Gauss-Hermite quadrature uses their roots as nodes.
tools.example:
HermiteH[3, x]
Table[HermiteH[n, x], {n, 0, 4}]
Integrate[HermiteH[2, x] HermiteH[2, x] Exp[-x^2], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]
HermiteH[4, 1.5]

tools.name: LaguerreL
tools.description: The Laguerre polynomials L_n(x) and, in the three-argument form, the generalized (associated) Laguerre polynomials L_n^a(x). They are orthogonal on [0, Infinity) with weight Exp[-x] x^a and give the radial part of hydrogen atom wavefunctions. They also provide the nodes for Gauss-Laguerre quadrature.
tools.example:
LaguerreL[2, x]
Table[LaguerreL[n, x], {n, 0, 3}]
LaguerreL[2, 1, x]
Integrate[LaguerreL[1, x]^2 Exp[-x], {x, 0, Infinity}]

tools.name: ChebyshevT
tools.description: The Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind T_n(x), satisfying T_n(Cos[t]) == Cos[n t]. ChebyshevU gives the second-kind polynomials. They minimize the maximum error in polynomial approximation, which makes them the basis of choice for spectral methods and near-minimax fits.
tools.example:
ChebyshevT[3, x]
ChebyshevT[5, Cos[t]] // TrigReduce
Table[ChebyshevT[n, x], {n, 0, 4}]
ChebyshevU[2, x]
N[Table[Cos[Pi (k - 1/2)/5], {k, 5}]]
tools.notes: The Chebyshev nodes Cos[Pi (2k-1)/(2n)] are the interpolation points that avoid Runge oscillation for high-degree polynomial interpolation.

tools.name: Hypergeometric2F1
tools.description: The Gauss hypergeometric function 2F1(a, b; c; z), which specializes to a very large fraction of the classical special functions. Solve, Integrate and DSolve often return results in this form. It has a branch cut from 1 to Infinity on the real axis.
tools.example:
Hypergeometric2F1[1, 1, 2, z]
Hypergeometric2F1[1/2, 1/2, 1, 0.5]
FunctionExpand[Hypergeometric2F1[1, 1, 2, z]]
Series[Hypergeometric2F1[a, b, c, z], {z, 0, 3}]
tools.notes: FunctionExpand or FullSimplify often rewrites a 2F1 into elementary functions when a special parameter relation holds.

tools.name: Hypergeometric1F1
tools.description: The confluent hypergeometric (Kummer) function 1F1(a; b; z), the limit of 2F1 as one parameter goes to infinity. It covers the incomplete gamma, error, Bessel and Laguerre functions as special cases and solves Kummer's differential equation. HypergeometricU is the second, logarithmically singular solution.
tools.usage:
Hypergeometric1F1[a, b, z]
HypergeometricU[a, b, z]
tools.example:
Hypergeometric1F1[1, 1, z]
Hypergeometric1F1[1, 2, z]
FunctionExpand[Hypergeometric1F1[1/2, 3/2, -z^2]]
HypergeometricU[1, 1, 2.]

tools.name: EllipticK
tools.description: The complete elliptic integral of the first kind K(m), using the parameter convention m == k^2. It gives the quarter period of a pendulum and appears in arc length computations for ellipses and lemniscates. EllipticF is the corresponding incomplete integral.
tools.example:
EllipticK[0]
EllipticK[0.5]
EllipticF[Pi/4, 0.5]
4 Sqrt[l/g] EllipticK[Sin[theta0/2]^2]
Series[EllipticK[m], {m, 0, 3}]
tools.notes: Wolfram Language uses the parameter m, not the modulus k; convert with m = k^2 when comparing with references that use k.

tools.name: EllipticE
tools.description: The complete elliptic integral of the second kind E(m), with the two-argument EllipticE[phi, m] giving the incomplete form. It gives the arc length of an ellipse and appears in surface area and potential calculations. Like EllipticK it uses the parameter convention m == k^2.
tools.example:
EllipticE[0]
EllipticE[0.5]
EllipticE[Pi/3, 0.5]
4 a EllipticE[1 - (b/a)^2]
ArcLength[{a Cos[t], b Sin[t]}, {t, 0, 2 Pi}]

tools.name: JacobiSN
tools.description: The Jacobi elliptic function sn(u, m), a doubly periodic generalization of the sine that reduces to Sin[u] when m == 0 and Tanh[u] when m == 1. JacobiCN, JacobiDN and the other nine Jacobi functions form the full family. They give the exact solution of the nonlinear pendulum and of many integrable systems.
tools.usage:
JacobiSN[u, m]
JacobiCN[u, m]
JacobiDN[u, m]
JacobiAmplitude[u, m]
tools.example:
JacobiSN[u, 0]
JacobiSN[1., 0.5]
JacobiCN[u, 1]
Simplify[JacobiSN[u, m]^2 + JacobiCN[u, m]^2]
Plot[JacobiSN[x, 0.9], {x, 0, 10}]

tools.name: WeierstrassP
tools.description: The Weierstrass elliptic function P(u; g2, g3), the doubly periodic function satisfying (P')^2 == 4 P^3 - g2 P - g3. WeierstrassPPrime gives its derivative and WeierstrassInvariants converts between period and invariant parametrizations. It is the canonical parametrization of an elliptic curve.
tools.usage:
WeierstrassP[u, {g2, g3}]
WeierstrassPPrime[u, {g2, g3}]
WeierstrassInvariants[{w1, w2}]
tools.example:
WeierstrassP[1., {1, 2}]
WeierstrassPPrime[1., {1, 2}]
WeierstrassInvariants[{1, I}]
Series[WeierstrassP[u, {g2, g3}], {u, 0, 4}]
